implementation_notes: The in-process default: one std::mutex per aggregate root, held in a registry keyed by the cluster id, plus an RAII guard (std::lock_guard or std::scoped_lock) for the duration of the edit so every exit path unlocks. The guard replaces the classic lock manager - the lock is a value whose lifetime is the critical section - and members are reached only through the cluster handle, never locked individually. Choose it for single-process servers that keep the cluster in memory; it does not coordinate other processes.

variants.name: std::mutex per aggregate root with an RAII guard
variants.implementation_notes: The in-process default: one std::mutex per aggregate root, held in a registry keyed by the cluster id, plus an RAII guard (std::lock_guard or std::scoped_lock) for the duration of the edit so every exit path unlocks. The guard replaces the classic lock manager - the lock is a value whose lifetime is the critical section - and members are reached only through the cluster handle, never locked individually. Choose it for single-process servers that keep the cluster in memory; it does not coordinate other processes.
pitfalls: A registry that returns a fresh mutex per call silently locks nothing; cache the shared_ptr per root id and never erase an entry that a thread may still hold.
Holding the cluster mutex while doing I/O or calling user callbacks turns a short critical section into a throughput cliff (and can re-enter the registry).

variants.name: root-row lock inside a transaction (libpqxx / ODBC / SQLite)
variants.implementation_notes: The durable default for multi-process deployments: inside one transaction, lock the aggregate root row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (PostgreSQL/MySQL) or an equivalent hint, then read and write every member; the root row is the lock identity, so no per-member lock is taken. The transaction boundary replaces the lock manager's bookkeeping - the database releases the lock on commit or rollback. Prefer it when several processes or hosts must serialise on the same cluster.
variants.idiom_name: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the root row through the C++ database client
pitfalls: A root row lock is released at transaction end, so an offline edit session cannot span user think time; use a lock table/version token for that case instead of holding transactions open.
Locking the root and then updating members in a different order across code paths reintroduces deadlocks - always go root first.
A registry that returns a fresh mutex per call silently locks nothing; cache the shared_ptr per root id and never erase an entry that a thread may still hold.
Holding the cluster mutex while doing I/O or calling user callbacks turns a short critical section into a throughput cliff (and can re-enter the registry).
